items.title: Understanding Time Measurement
items.explanation: Humans have tracked time by observing natural cycles like the rising and setting of the Sun, phases of the Moon, and seasons. These observations led to the creation of calendars based on daily solar cycles. Before mechanical clocks, people used simple devices like sundials (measuring shadow), water clocks (flowing water), hourglasses (sand flow), and candle clocks (burning time) to measure smaller intervals within a day.

items.title: Ancient Timekeeping Devices
items.explanation: In ancient India, time was measured using shadows from vertical sticks (Arthasastra) and water clocks described in texts like Arthasastra. While early water clocks were inaccurate due to changing flow rates, the sinking bowl clock (Ghatika-yantra) by Aryabhata improved accuracy. This device used a floating bowl that sank when filled, triggering drums or conch shells to announce time passage.

items.title: Evolution of Mechanical Time
items.explanation: As travel increased and civilisation advanced, mechanical devices using weights, gears, and springs became critical. The invention of the pendulum clock in the seventeenth century marked a major breakthrough, providing more accurate timekeeping compared to earlier mechanical methods.

items.title: Prerna's Goal
items.explanation: Prerna dreams of representing India at the international level in 100 metre sprint contests. She trains to compete at the state level and hopes to win an interschool competition, aiming for future representation.

items.title: Activity: Constructing a Water Clock
items.explanation: To build a water clock, cut a 1/2 litre plastic bottle in half. Make a small hole in the cap and place the upper part inverted over the lower part. Fill the top with water (adding ink for visibility). When the water drips into the bottom, mark the level every minute until it empties.

items.title: Fascinating Fact: The Samrat Yantra
items.explanation: The world's largest stone sundial, the Samrat Yantra, was built around 300 years ago in Jaipur. It has a height of 27 metres and measures local time intervals as short as 2 seconds.
